fixes.title: Give the AI the expert's declaration
fixes.root_cause: The AI read each answer in isolation. When an expert said “we”, “their” or “the board”, it could not tell which company was meant, so it missed that the expert was talking about their own employer, a client or a former employer.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: Thanks for joining, Expert 3429. I'm looking at UK grocery supply chains, especially cold chain and automation. Can you start with how the landscape has changed over the last five years?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: Sure. The big shift is that the large grocers stopped treating distribution as a cost centre and started treating it as a competitive weapon. Before the pandemic, most of the conversation was about squeezing pennies out of each case. After 2020, it became about resilience. Everyone saw empty shelves and realised a lean network has no slack.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: What did that mean in practice?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: More regional depots, more safety stock on key lines, and a lot more investment in visibility. You'd be amazed how many grocers, even large ones, didn't know where a pallet was between leaving the supplier and arriving at the depot. Now most of the big players have some kind of control tower, a single view of inbound freight.

turns.speaker: INTERVIEWER
turns.text: And automation?

turns.speaker: EXPERT
turns.text: It's real, but it's uneven. Automated picking works brilliantly for ambient goods, tins, pasta, that kind of thing. Chilled is harder because of temperature and shelf life, and fresh produce is harder still because items are irregular. So you see grocers automate ambient first and keep people on chilled and fresh.
